segments.text: When I assemble charges I have to do work, we discussed that earlier and we call that electrostatic potential energy.
Today I will look at this energy concept in a different way and I will evaluate the energy in terms of the electric field.

Suppose I have two parallel plates and I charge this one with positive charge which is the surface charge density times the area of the plate $+Q = +\sigma A$ and this one negative charge which is the surface charge density negative times the area of the plate $-Q = -\sigma A$.
And let's assume that the separation between these two is $h$ and so we have an electric field which is approximately constant and the electric field here $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.
And now I'm going to take the upper plate and I'm going to move it up.
And so as I do that I have to apply a force because these two plates attract each other so I have to do work.
And as I move this up and I will move it up over a distance $x$.
I am creating here electric field that wasn't there before.

And the electric field $E$ that I'm creating has exactly the same strength as this $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ because the charge on the plates is not changing when I'm moving, the surface charge density $\sigma$ is not changing, all I do is I increase the distance.
And so I am creating electric field in here.
And for that I have to do work, that's another way of looking at it.
How much work do I have to do, what is the work $W_{WL}$ that Walter Lewin has to do in moving this plate over a distance $x$?
Well that is the force $F_{WL}$ that I have to apply over that distance $x$.
The force is constant and so I can simply multiply the force times the distance that would give me work $W_{WL} = F_{WL}x$.
And so the question now is what is the force $F_{WL}$ that I have to apply to move this plate up?

And your first guess would be that the force $F_{WL}$ would be the charge on the plate $Q$ times the electric field strength $E$, a complete reasonable guess because you would argue, well if we have an electric field $E$ and we bring a charge $Q$ in there then the electric force is $Q \times E$, I have to overcome that force so my force is $Q \times E$.
Yes, that holds most of the time but not in this case, it's a little bit more subtle.
Let me take this plate here and enlarge that plate.
So here is the plate, so you see the thickness of the plate now, this is one plate.

We all agree that the plus charge is at the surface, well but of course it has to be in the plate and so there is here this layer of charge $+Q$ which is at the bottom of the plate and the thickness of that layer may only be one atomic thickness but it's not zero.
And on this side of the plate is that electric field $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ but inside the plate which is a conductor the electric field $E$ is $0$.
And therefore the electric field in this charge $Q$ is the average between the two.
And so the force on this charge in this layer is not $Q \times E$ but it's $\frac{1}{2}QE$.
So I take the average between these E fields and this $E$ field is then this value $\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.
And so now I can calculate the work that I have to do.
The work that I have to do is now my force $F_{WL} = \frac{1}{2}QE$ and I move that over a distance $x$.
And so what I can do now is replace $Q$ by $\sigma A$ so I get $W_{WL} = \frac{1}{2}\sigma AE \times x$.
And I multiply upstairs and downstairs by $\varepsilon_0$ so that I multiply by one.
And the reason why I do that is because then I get another $\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ here and that is $E$.
And therefore I now have that the total work $W_{WL}$ that I Walter Lewin have to do is $\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 Ax$.
And look at this, $Ax$ is the new volume that I have created, it is the new volume in which I have created electric field.
And this now calls for a work done by Walter Lewin per unit volume $\frac{W_{WL}}{\text{volume}}$ and that now equals $\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$.
This is the work that I have done per unit volume and since this work created electric field we call it field energy density and it is in Joules per cubic meter $J/m^3$.
And it can be shown that in general the electric field energy density is $\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$ not only for this particular charge configuration but for any charge configuration.
And so now we have a new way of looking at the energy that it takes to assemble charges.

Earlier we calculated the work that we have to do to put the charges in place, now if it is more convenient we could calculate that the energy, the electrostatic potential energy $U$, is the integral $U = \int \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 dV$ of $\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$ over all space if necessary you have to go all the way down to infinity and here I have now $dV$, this is volume.
This has nothing to do with potential, this $V$ in physics we often run out of symbols, $V$ is sometimes potential, in this case it is volume.
And the only reason why I chose $h$ there is...
I already already have a $d$ here, and so I didn't want two $d$s; normally we take $d$ as the separation between plates.
And so this now is another way of looking at electrostatic potential energy $U = \int \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E^2 d\tau$.
We look at it now only from the point of view of all the energy being in the electric field $E$, and we no longer think of it, perhaps, as the work that you have done to assemble these charges.
I will demonstrate later today that as I separate the two plates from these charged planes that indeed I have to do work.
I will convince you that by creating electric field $E$ that indeed I will be doing work.
So from now on, we have the choice.

If you want to calculate what the electrostatic potential energy is, you either calculate the work that you have to do to bring all these charges in place or, if it is easy, you can take the electric field $E$ everywhere in space, if you know that, and do an integration over all space.
We could do that for instance for these two parallel plates now, and we can ask, what is now the total energy in the field?

And at home I would advise you to do that the way that is done in your book, whereby you actually assemble the charges $-Q$ at the bottom and $+Q$ at the top and you calculate how much work you have to do.

That's one approach. I will now choose the other approach, and that is by simply saying that the total energy $U$ in the field of these plane parallel plates is the integral $U = \int \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E^2 d\tau$ over the entire volume of these two plates.
And since the electric field $E$ is outside zero everywhere, it's a very easy integral, because I know the volume.
The volume that I have, if the separation is $h$—so we still have them $h$ apart—this volume that I have is simply $A \times h$.

And the electric field $E$ is constant, and so I get here that this $U$ is $\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0$—for $E$, if I want to, I can write $\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$, I can square that $(\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0})^2$—and $dV$ doing the integral over all space means simply I get $A \times h$.
It is the volume of that box, so I get $A \times h$.
And so this is now the total energy that I have.
I lose one $\varepsilon$ here, I have an $\varepsilon_0^2$ and I have an $\varepsilon$.

I also remember that the charge $Q$ on the plate is $A \times \sigma$ and that the potential difference $V$—this now is not volume, it's the potential difference between the plates—is the electric field $E$ times $h$.
The electric field $E$ is constant, as we go from one plate to the other.
The integral $\int E \cdot dl$ in going from one plate to the other gives me the potential difference $V$.
And so I can substitute that now in here; I can take for $A \times \sigma$, I can put in the $Q$.
And you can also show that this $U$ is $\frac{1}{2} QV$, $V$ being now the potential difference between the plates.

And so this is a rather fast way that you can calculate what the total energy is in the field, or to say the same thing, the total work you have to do to assemble these charges, or to say it differently, the total work you have to do to create electric fields $E$.
You have created electric fields $E$ that were not there before.
I now will introduce something that we haven't had before, and that is the word capacitance.
I will define the capacitance $C = \frac{Q}{V}$ of an object to be the charge $Q$ of that object divided by the potential $V$ of that object.
And so the unit is Coulombs per Volt—this $V$ is Volt now, it's potential—but we never say that it is Coulomb per Volt in physics.
We write for that a capital $F$, which is Farad.
We call that 1 Farad is the unit of capacitance, undoubtedly called after the great maestro Faraday; we will learn more about Faraday later in this course.
So let us go to a sphere which has a radius $R$ and let us calculate what the capacitance $C$ is of this sphere.
Think of it as being a conductor, and we bring a certain charge $Q$ on this conductor.
It will then get a potential $V$ which we know is $V = \frac{Q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R}$.
We've seen it many times, and so by definition, the capacitance $C = \frac{Q}{V}$ now is $Q$ divided by the potential and therefore this becomes $4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R$.
So that is the capacitance $C$ of a single sphere.
And so we can now look at the values as a function of $R$.
I have here some numbers; I calculated it for the Van de Graaff, and I calculated it for the Earth.
If you want one Farad capacitance—that's a real biggie—you need a radius $R$ of $9 \times 10^9$ meters; that's the $4 \pi \varepsilon_0$ that comes in there.
That's huge; that's 25 times the distance from the Earth to the moon; that's a big sphere, would have a capacitance of one Farad.
The Earth itself with a radius $R$ of $6400$ kilometers would have $700$ microFarads.
The Van de Graaff, $30$ centimeters radius $R$, would be $30$ picoFarads—a pico is $10^{-12}$.
And if you take a sphere with a radius $R$ of $1$ centimeter, then you have roughly $1$ picoFarad, $10^{-12}$ Farads.
So this gives you a rough idea about the size of objects and how they connect to their capacitance $C$.
So if I bring all these spheres at the same potential—
So I charge them all up to the same potential, then the one with the largest capacitance will have the most charge.
And that of course is where the word capacitance comes from; it is the capability of holding charge for a given electric potential.

Don't confuse that with electric fields, because if you bring all these spheres at the same potential, then the one with the strongest electric field, that's the one which has the smallest radius—we discussed that last time.
Now I will look at the situation a little bit differently.
I have here a sphere $B$ positively charged, and I place it close to another sphere $A$ which is negatively charged.
And so by my definition, I can say that the capacitance of $B$ $C_B$ is the charge that I have on $B$ $Q_B$ divided by the potential of $B$ $V_B$.
That would be my definition.
But there is here this object $A$ which charge negative.
And how did we define potential?
Potential was work per unit charge.
I go to infinity, I put $+q$ in my pocket, I approach $B$ and the work I have to do per unit charge is the potential of $B$ $V_B$—that's the definition of potential.
But $B$ is repelling me, so I have to do positive work, but $A$ is now attracting me.
And so the work I have to do is less, the work per unit charge.
And so because of the presence of $A$, the potential of $B$ $V_B$ goes down and therefore the capacitance of $B$ $C_B$ goes up.
And so now you see that the presence of this charged sphere $A$ here has an influence, an important impact on the capacitance of $B$.
And therefore it is really unfair to call this $C_B$ the capacitance of $B$.
We think of it as the capacitance of $B$ in the presence of $A$.
So it's no longer just $B$ alone.
And so I'm now going to change the definition of capacitance.
And I'm going to change it in the following way.
I have two conductors.
And these two conductors have the same charge but different polarities.

And now the capacitance of this combination of two conductors $C = \frac{\text{charge}}{\text{potential diff}}$ is the charge on one of them, which is the same of course on the charge of the other except different polarity, divided by the potential difference.
So that $C = \frac{\text{charge}}{\text{potential diff}}$ now is my new definition of capacitance.
So we always deal with two objects, not with one in isolation.
If you have the charge on one of the two and you divide it by the potential difference between the two.
You may say, "Well, it's a little artificial to have two conductors and one is positively charged and the other has exactly the same amount of negatively charged."
Well, it is not so artificial as you may think.
Remember when we had this Wimshurst machine which I was cranking, and I was charging one plate positive and the other one negative?
Without my doing anything, if one becomes positive, the other one becomes negative by exactly the same amount, because you cannot create charge out of nothing.
So if you charge one thing positive, chances are that something else is charged negative by the same amount but with opposite polarity.
So it's not too artificial that you have two conductors with the same charge but opposite polarities.
So now we have two conductors there.
So if we go to this—these two parallel plates—the question now is: what is now the capacitance then according to our new definition of these parallel plates?
Well, that capacitance $C$ is the charge on one plate $Q$ divided by the potential difference between the two plates $V$.
And the charge on one plate $Q$ is $\sigma A$.
And the potential difference between the plates $V$ is the integral of $\int E \cdot dl$.
They are separated there by a distance $h$.
I will change that now to a $d$ because that's more commonly done, that the separation between plates is $d$.
There was a reason why I didn't want to put a $d$ there, because I didn't want to get you confused, but now there is no confusion.
And so the potential difference $V$ is the electric field between the plates $E$ times the distance $d$.
But $E$ itself is $\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.
So we get here $C = \frac{\sigma A \varepsilon_0}{\sigma d}$.
I lose my $\sigma$. And so two parallel plates have this $\frac{A \varepsilon_0}{d}$ as the capacitance.
It's linearly proportional with the area of the plates $A$.
That's intuitively pleasing: the larger the plate, the more charge you can put on there.
And it's inversely proportional with the distance between the plates $d$.
The smaller you make the distance, the larger is the capacitance.
Well, that goes back to this idea that the closer $A$ is to $B$, the larger effect that will have on the capacitance.
And if you bring them very close together, this potential $V_B$ will go down and so the capacitance $C_B$ will go up.
So it's not too surprising that you see $d$ here downstairs.
The closer you bring the plates together, the higher the capacitance will be.

Well, we already calculated that.
We had the energy, this $U = \dots = \frac{1}{2}QV$ was the plate capacitor $\frac{1}{2}QV$.
And we can now substitute in there the capacitance $C$, and the $C = \frac{Q}{V}$ is $Q$ divided by $V$ and so this is also $\frac{1}{2}CV^2$.
That's one and the same thing. So either you take the charge on the capacitor multiplied by $V$ or you take the capacitance multiplied by a $V^2$.

Here if you look here, the capacitance $\text{Farad} = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$ is only a matter of geometry.

And that means that the $\frac{1}{2}CV^2$, the energy stored then in that capacitor, will be $25\text{J}$.
And I can dump that energy over the light bulb, and then we see a bright flash of light,
because this discharge can occur in something like only a millisecond,
so you get a tremendous amount of light only for that millisecond.
And I want to demonstrate that to you.
And the only way I can demonstrate that to you is by aiming this flashlight at you.
I don't want to damage your eyes, so I warn you in advance.
So I am charging up now my capacitor; will take a while, and I'm going to take your picture — I might as well.
But it's going to be very dark in the back there,
and so I've asked Marcos and Bill to also have some flashlights, which go off at the same time that my flashlight goes off.
Now you may say, 'Well, how can you do that?' because if this flash only lasts a millisecond, how can you synchronize that?
Well, the way that's done is that those flashlights are waiting for my light signal to reach them.
And that goes with the speed of light; takes way less than a millisecond to get there.
And they go at the same time that they receive my light flash.
And so we call them flash assists.
And so let's see whether we can do this.
I have a green light here, that means I can take my picture.
Oh, you don't have to comb your hair, but you're looking good.
Okay, let me focus because that's important.
So make sure you see the flash; you ready for this?
Did you see the flash? Did it flash? Oh, it did — you can say yes.
So did the light assist also flash?
Okay, but you haven't seen that yet, right? Because you were looking at them; you really should have looked at me.
So why don't we take a picture — Marcos, Bill, aim the flash assist at the students here and then we'll try it again.
You ready? Okay.
Oh, why don't you say 'cheese' for a change?
Okay, look at me; oh boy, you're looking great, you really — oh, I'm out of focus.
There's one person sleeping there, we'll let him sleep; that's okay, thank you.
Did that work? Did you see the flash? You did, hey?
$25\text{J}$! But those haven't seen it yet.
So Marcos and Bill, make sure that we go this way and give them a chance to see this light flash.
So we get a little bit of assistance there of the light.
And let's see how this works; make sure that you see the flash.
Very good; you're going to see another $25\text{J}$ going through this light bulb.
Very good, oh, oh, oh, yeah, yeah; your hand is in front of your mouth, sir; yeah, that's okay, thank you.
Very good; did you see the flash? Did the assist go?
So that's the idea of photoflashes.
So you dump a lot of energy in a very short amount of time, and you get a very bright flash.
Professor Edgerton at MIT became very famous for his flashlights.
He invented flashes that can handle way more energy than this flash,
and they can dump that energy in less than one microsecond.
And so this opened up the road to high-speed photography,
and that made it possible to study the motion of objects on time scales of microseconds and even shorter than that.
And I'd like to show you some of the pictures that were taken with Doc Edgerton's flashes.
You see a bullet coming from the right, going for a light bulb.
The exposure of this picture is only $\frac{1}{3}$ microsecond,
during which the bullet probably moved only $\frac{1}{3}$ millimeter, so it looks like it's completely standing still.
And the bulb is heading for disaster, but it doesn't know that yet.
The bullet moves in $100$ microseconds about $8\text{cm}$.
And the next picture is taken $100$ microseconds later, again $\frac{1}{3}$ microsecond exposure.
So if we can look at that, there you see — so the bullet now just penetrates the light bulb.
And then the next picture is another $100$ microseconds later, and there you see the bullet emerging from the light bulb.
And this light bulb has hardly realized that it is broken.
But it's beginning to dawn on it and —
And then the next slide is one wonderful picture of a boy who's popping a balloon,
and you see half the balloon doesn't even know yet that it is broken.
Doc Edgerton also developed a lot of strobes.
A strobe — I have one here — is an instrument that repeatedly discharges energy over a light bulb.
And so you get repeated flashes.
And that then gives you the instrument like this.
You've seen them in use; they're being used at airplanes just for warning signals,
and you've also seen them on tall towers near airports, also warning signals.
But there are a lot more things you can do with strobes.
And later in 8.02, I will show you, for instance, that you can measure the rotation rate of motors with flashlights, with these stroboscopes.
And motors are going to play a more important role in 8.02 than you may have guessed before you took this course.
You can also measure with strobes the rotation, the speed of your record player, if you still have one,
and then you can adjust it so that it just has the right speed that is required.
So there are a lot of things you can do with strobes, and some of which we will see also in 8.02.
My capacitor there. And let's see how it is doing.
Oh, boy, we're close to the $3000$ which was my goal.
It takes, you see, a good $15$ minutes to actually reach the $3000$ volts on this huge capacitor and to get in there the energy, the $450$ joules that I wanted.
And why is it that I want to show you this? Well, I want you to appreciate the idea of a fuse.
You have lots of fuses at home. A fuse is a safety device.
A fuse is something that melts, something that breaks, if the current that you are using is too high.

Suppose you have a short, electric short without realizing it in your desk lamp and a very high current could start to flow, then the fuse will say, "Sorry, you can't do that," the fuse will melt and then that's—prevents you from a disaster which actually might give you a fire.
And we already showed in a way the idea of a fuse because when we broke this light bulb, that was in a way a fuse.
We dumped too much energy through that light bulb, and so the light bulb itself was already like a fuse.
This is really more like a fuse that we are used to.
We have a wire there which is an iron wire which is $12$ inches long and it has a thickness of $30$ thousandths of an inch.

So the idea is very much like we had the photo flash.

Three, two, one, zero.

I'm going to short it out with this conducting bar and see whether we can get a spark.
And we can. So there's still some energy left.
Okay. See you Friday.

sections.title: Electric Field Energy Density
sections.description: The instructor derives the energy density formula by calculating the work required to separate two charged parallel plates.

sections.title: Fundamental Definition of Capacitance
sections.description: Capacitance is defined as the ratio of charge to potential and calculated for spheres of various sizes.

sections.title: Systems of Two Conductors
sections.description: The lecture explains how neighboring charges affect potential and redefines capacitance for a two-conductor configuration.

sections.title: Physical Properties of Capacitors
sections.description: The instructor examines the internal construction of rolled-up commercial capacitors and discusses their energy storage capabilities.

sections.title: Potential Difference and Work
sections.description: A demonstration shows that increasing plate separation does work and raises the potential difference between the plates.

sections.title: Capacitor Discharge and Photo Flashes
sections.description: The class observes energy discharge through light bulbs to understand the operational principles behind photographic flash units.

sections.title: High Speed Photography and Strobes
sections.description: Dr. Harold Edgerton’s contributions to high-speed strobe photography are presented through images of bullets and balloons.

sections.title: Energy Discharge and Fuse Mechanics
sections.description: The lecture concludes by melting a wire with a high-energy capacitor to demonstrate how electrical fuses function.
